Research-Engineer Curriculum

Volume 2: The Researcher's Experiment Loop

Volume 2: The Researcher's Experiment Loop

How to run an experiment you can trust, and how to tell when you cannot. The refresher taught you how models train. This volume teaches you how researchers decide what is true: the experiment loop, honest splits, metrics that do not lie, leakage detection, and the statistics of "did we actually win." Every chapter ends with a lab you run on your own machine.

Assumed known: Volume 1 math (MLE, bias-variance, gradients) and the ML/DL refresher (train/val/test by name, accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC, SGD, momentum, Adam). Forward links: Volume 4 puts normalization and mixed precision to work at transformer scale; Volume 11 builds full evaluation methodology for LLM systems on top of the statistics in Chapter 5.

Last verified: September 2026. Live-verified: Guo et al., "On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks" (ICML 2017, arXiv:1706.04599) for temperature scaling; every lab number and figure in this volume comes from local NumPy runs executed September 2026 (outputs quoted verbatim); internet diagrams credited to CampusAI (5-fold cross-validation) and ds100.org, UC Berkeley (split pipeline). UNVERIFIED: none. Statements about common field conventions (for example, k = 5 as a usual default for folds) are labeled as conventions, not findings.

Chapter 1: The Experiment Loop

Design prompt

  • What is the smallest unit of a research result?
  • Why does a single training run mean nothing?
  • What is an ablation, and why does it beat "I tried everything at once"?
  • What belongs in a lab notebook entry for one experiment?

1.1 The loop: hypothesis, baseline, intervention, measure, decide

A research result is not a number. It is a controlled comparison: one thing changed, everything else held fixed, the difference measured with uncertainty. The unit that produces such comparisons is the experiment loop, and it has five steps. First, a hypothesis: a falsifiable claim, for example "adding squared features helps this classifier because the true boundary is curved." Second, a baseline: the simplest credible setup, trained and measured before the idea touches it. Third, the intervention: exactly one change. Fourth, measurement on data the decision did not touch, with error bars. Fifth, a decision: ship, iterate, or kill.

Why this discipline exists: training is noisy. Seeds, data order, and hardware nondeterminism move results by fractions of a point, and a "win" smaller than that noise is not a win. The loop exists to separate signal from that noise. Under the hood, think of it as a state machine where each step constrains the next: the hypothesis constrains what you are allowed to conclude, the baseline constrains what the intervention is compared against, and the measurement step constrains whether the decision is even licensed.

Concrete numbers: in Lab 2.1 the baseline (linear features) reaches 87.34% mean accuracy over 8 seeds with a standard deviation of 0.75 points, while the intervention (adding squared features) reaches 94.65% with standard deviation 0.57. The delta is +7.31 percentage points, roughly ten times the noise. That ratio, delta over noise, is the entire game.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Start at Hypothesis (navy): a falsifiable claim, not a wish. It must be specific enough that data could prove it wrong.
  2. Baseline (blue): train and measure the simplest credible setup first. No idea gets tested without one.
  3. Intervention (teal): change exactly one variable. The loop is a scalpel, not a blender.
  4. Measure (amber): evaluate on held-out data, across seeds, with spread reported. One run is an anecdote.
  5. Decide (coral): ship, iterate, or kill. Then the arrow feeds the decision back into a new hypothesis.

Common misunderstanding: "My idea works" is not a result. A result is "the intervention beats the baseline by X ± Y, and I know which part of the intervention caused it." If you changed three things at once, you have a demo, not an experiment.

"A research result is a controlled comparison: one thing changed, everything else fixed, the difference measured with uncertainty."

Q1. You run your new architecture once and beat the baseline by 0.4 points. Your colleague is unconvinced. Who is right, and what is the cheapest next step?

Answer: your colleague. One run cannot separate a 0.4-point delta from seed noise (Lab 2.1 shows seed std near 0.75 points on a toy problem). The cheapest next step is to re-run both baseline and intervention over a handful of seeds and check whether the delta survives.

1.2 Baselines and ablations: attributing credit

A baseline is the simplest thing that could work, and it is the most underrated object in ML. A weak baseline makes any idea look good; a strong baseline is what makes a positive result mean something. When you read a paper, check the baselines first: if the proposed method beats a baseline that was tuned with one tenth of the effort, the comparison is theater.

An ablation removes one component of a system to measure its contribution. The name comes from biology: remove the part, see what breaks. The discipline is one variable at a time. If your model has a new attention block, a new loss, and a new schedule, and the full system wins, you do not know which piece won. The ablation ladder below shows the standard pattern: full system at the top, then one row per removed component, then the bare baseline at the bottom.

Ablation ladder (each row changes ONE thing vs the row above)
================================================================
 full system:  new block + new loss + new schedule      94.6%
   - new schedule (keep block, keep loss)               93.9%   (-0.7)
   - new loss     (keep block, old loss)                92.1%   (-1.8)
   - new block    (old block, old loss, old schedule)    87.3%   baseline
================================================================
Credit: the block is worth ~4.8pp, the loss ~1.8pp, the schedule ~0.7pp.
Kill the schedule if it costs complexity; keep the block.

Why this matters under the hood: components interact, so removal order can change the numbers, but the ladder still bounds each component's marginal value. Run the ladder in the order you would actually delete things in production: most expensive or most complex first. Concrete numbers from Lab 2.1: the single intervention (squared features) moved accuracy from 87.34% to 94.65%, a +7.31 point delta with the min over seeds (93.70%) still far above the baseline's max (88.60%). No overlap between the distributions: that is what a real effect looks like.

Common misunderstanding: an ablation is not a hyperparameter sweep. A sweep asks "what setting is best"; an ablation asks "does this component earn its place." Also, "ablating" by adding components one at a time to a weak baseline inflates every component's apparent value. Remove from the full system instead.

"Remove from the full system, one piece at a time. The ladder tells you which components earn their complexity."

1.3 Lab 2.1: the experiment harness

Lab 2.1: experiment harness (labs/lab_2_1_experiment_harness.py)

A minimal honest runner: one baseline, one intervention, 8 fixed seeds each, identical data splits. The true signal has a quadratic term, so adding squared features is a genuine intervention. Pure NumPy, CPU only, finishes in seconds.

def run_experiment(name, transform, seeds, l2=1.0):
    """One variable changes between experiments: `transform`.
    Everything else (data split, optimizer, seeds) is identical."""
    X, y = make_data()
    ...
    for s in seeds:
        rng = np.random.default_rng(1000 + s)
        idx = rng.permutation(n)
        Xtr, ytr = X[idx[:3000]], y[idx[:3000]]
        Xva, yva = X[idx[3000:]], y[idx[3000:]]
        w, b = train_logreg(transform(Xtr), ytr, l2=l2, seed=s)
        accs.append(accuracy(w, b, transform(Xva), yva))
    ...

Captured output (verbatim):

experiment                                mean    std     min     max
baseline: linear features               87.34%  0.75%  86.00%  88.60%
intervention: + squared features        94.65%  0.57%  93.70%  95.40%

Intervention delta: +7.31 pp (mean over 8 seeds each)
How to read this diagram.
  1. Two bars: the gray baseline and the blue intervention. Height is mean accuracy over 8 seeds.
  2. The whiskers are one standard deviation across seeds: the noise floor of this setup.
  3. The gap between the bars (+7.31 points) dwarfs the whiskers. When the delta is many times the noise, the decision is easy. Chapter 5 is about the cases where it is not.

Key takeaways

  • The smallest unit of a research result is a controlled comparison, not a number.
  • Run every experiment over multiple seeds and report mean with spread.
  • Change one variable at a time; use the ablation ladder to attribute credit.
  • Tune the baseline as hard as the idea, or the comparison is theater.

Chapter 2: Splits Done Right

Design prompt

  • Why do we need three splits instead of two?
  • When is a random split a lie?
  • What does k-fold cross-validation buy you, and what does it cost?
  • What is nested cross-validation, and when do you need it?

2.1 Train, validation, test: the two-stage split

You need three splits because you make two different kinds of decisions. The validation set is for decisions: which hyperparameters, which checkpoint, which architecture. The test set is for the final unbiased estimate, used once, after all decisions are frozen. If you tune on the test set, it becomes a second validation set and your "unbiased" estimate is biased. The procedure is two-stage: first lock the test set away, then split what remains into train and validation.

Under the hood, every decision you make on validation data leaks a little information about that data into your model. Pick the best of 50 hyperparameter settings on validation and you have fit 50 configurations to it; the winning score is optimistic. The test set exists to measure the cost of all those decisions exactly once. This is why the refresher's basic split picture is only the start: the discipline is about what you are allowed to do with each split, not just their sizes.

Concrete numbers from Lab 2.2: the same model on the same data scores 75.93% under a random split, 72.23% under a group split, and 66.83% under a temporal split. The split is a modeling decision, and the honest one can cost you 9 points.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Left: the full dataset. The first arrow is the train-test split: the test block (orange) is separated and locked. Nothing you do afterward may touch it.
  2. Middle: the remaining training data (blue). The second arrow is the validation split: carve validation out of train, never out of test.
  3. The order matters. Test first, then validation. Reversing the order is how test information leaks into model selection.

Common misunderstanding: "I will just use the test set for early stopping, it is only one decision." Every decision on test data spends some of its unbiasedness. Early stopping on test is tuning on test. Keep a validation split for it.

"Lock the test set first, decide on validation, measure once. The test set is a budget you spend exactly once."

2.2 Cross-validation: stable estimates from small data

k-fold cross-validation splits the data into k equal parts, trains on k-1, evaluates on the remaining one, and rotates so every part serves as the evaluation fold once. The reported score is the mean over folds, and the spread across folds is a direct measurement of how much the score depends on which data you happened to hold out. Use it when data is scarce or when a single split's luck could dominate the conclusion.

What it costs: k full training runs. With k = 5, a common convention, you pay 5x the compute of a single split. What it buys: an estimate whose variance you can see. Under the hood, the folds are not independent (training sets overlap), so the spread across folds slightly understates the true variance, but it is far more honest than a single number. After cross-validation, the standard practice is to refit the chosen configuration on all the data before the final test evaluation.

Nested cross-validation is the careful version: an outer loop measures generalization while an inner loop does model selection. You need it when the model selection itself is aggressive (many configurations) and you want an unbiased estimate of the whole pipeline. It costs k_outer times k_inner runs, so reserve it for small data and high-stakes decisions.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Each of the five rows is one complete training run. The data is cut into five equal blocks.
  2. In row 1, block 1 (orange) is the validation fold and blocks 2-5 (blue) train. In row 2, block 2 validates, and so on down the rows.
  3. Five scores come out, one per row. Report their mean and spread. The spread is the honest part: it tells you how much the score wobbles with the data split.

Common misunderstanding: cross-validation does not fix leakage. If your preprocessing or your split leaks, all k folds leak identically and the mean looks confidently wrong. Fix the split first (Chapter 4), then average.

"Cross-validation buys you a visible variance at k times the cost. It never fixes a leaking split."

2.3 Lab 2.2: the split shootout

Lab 2.2: split shootout (labs/lab_2_2_split_shootout.py)

One drifting dataset, one model, three split strategies. The data distribution shifts over time, so a random split mixes past and future in both train and test, while the temporal split trains on the past and tests on the future: the deployment question.

Captured output (verbatim):

strategy                                          test acc
random split                                       75.93% (+/- 1.43)
temporal split (train past, test future)           66.83% (+/- 0.00)
group split (whole time blocks held out)           72.23% (+/- 2.12)

Same model, same data. The random split is optimistic because
train and test share the same time mix. The temporal split asks
the honest question: does it still work TOMORROW?
How to read this diagram.
  1. Three bars, one model, one dataset. Only the split strategy changes.
  2. Random is highest because train and test share the same time mix: the test contains patterns the model already saw in training.
  3. Temporal is lowest and most honest for deployment: it asks whether the model works on the future it has never seen.
  4. Takeaway for reviews: when someone reports a number, your first question is "what was the split."

Key takeaways

  • Lock test away first, decide on validation, spend the test budget once.
  • Match the split to the deployment question: temporal for time, group for grouped data.
  • k-fold CV gives you a visible variance at k times the compute; refit on all data afterward.
  • Leakage poisons every fold equally, so fix the split before averaging.

Chapter 3: Metrics Beyond Accuracy

Design prompt

  • When does accuracy lie to you?
  • Read a confusion matrix: which cell hurts you most depends on what?
  • What does perplexity actually measure, in one sentence?
  • What is calibration, and why should you care before shipping a classifier?

3.1 Precision, recall, F1: when accuracy lies

Accuracy is the fraction of correct predictions. It lies whenever the classes are imbalanced or the errors have unequal costs. A fraud detector that says "not fraud" on every transaction is 99.9% accurate and completely useless. The confusion matrix is the antidote: it breaks predictions into true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives, and every serious metric is arithmetic on those four cells.

Precision is TP / (TP + FP): of the times the model cried wolf, how often was there a wolf. Recall is TP / (TP + FN): of the real wolves, how many did it catch. The F1 score is their harmonic mean, which punishes a model that sacrifices one for the other. Under the hood, the harmonic mean is the right average here because precision and recall are rates; the arithmetic mean would let a model with 100% precision and 0% recall score 50%.

Concrete numbers from Lab 2.3 (2,800 test samples): TP = 1214, FP = 253, FN = 215, TN = 1118. Precision = 1214 / (1214 + 253) = 0.828. Recall = 1214 / (1214 + 215) = 0.850. F1 = 0.838. The accuracy is 83.29%, but the matrix tells you the shape of the errors: 253 false alarms against 215 missed positives.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Rows are the truth, columns are the prediction. Top-left (TP = 1214): actually positive, predicted positive. Bottom-right (TN = 1118): actually negative, predicted negative.
  2. Top-right (FP = 253): false alarms. Bottom-left (FN = 215): missed positives. Which cell hurts more is a product decision, not a math decision.
  3. Precision reads down the left column: 1214 / (1214 + 253). Recall reads across the top row: 1214 / (1214 + 215).

Common misunderstanding: optimizing F1 is not the same as optimizing the business objective. F1 weights precision and recall equally; your product almost certainly does not. Pick the metric that matches the cost of errors, and say so out loud.

"Accuracy is a summary; the confusion matrix is the story. Pick the metric that matches the cost of being wrong."

Q2. A cancer screening model has 99% accuracy. Why might a doctor still reject it, and which single number would you show first instead?

Answer: with 1% prevalence, a model that always says "healthy" hits 99% accuracy while catching zero cancers. Show recall first: of the actual cancers, how many did it catch. A screening test that misses the disease is worse than useless.

3.2 Perplexity and calibration: the two numbers LLMs live by

Perplexity is the standard metric of language modeling: the exponential of the average cross-entropy per token. In one sentence, it measures how surprised the model is by real text. If the model assigns probability p to each true next token, the per-token surprise is -ln(p), the average surprise is the cross-entropy H, and perplexity is e^H. Lower is better: a perplexity of 20 means the model is as confused as if it were choosing uniformly among 20 tokens at each step.

Under the hood, perplexity is just cross-entropy wearing an exponential. Worked example: the model sees "the cat sat on the" and assigns 0.68 to "mat", 0.22 to "rug", 0.10 to "moon". If the true token is "mat", that token contributes -ln(0.68) = 0.386 nats of surprise. Average over the corpus, exponentiate, and you have perplexity. The number compounds multiplicatively, which is why small per-token improvements move it a lot.

Calibration asks a different question: when the model says 80% confident, is it right 80% of the time? A model can have excellent perplexity and terrible calibration, confidently wrong on the tokens that matter. Modern networks are systematically overconfident: they memorize the training set, push logits to extremes, and report probabilities near 1.0 on test inputs they get wrong. Calibration matters the moment a probability drives a decision: abstention thresholds, human review queues, anything with a cost.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Top row: the context tokens the model has seen. The arrow is the prediction step.
  2. Three candidate next words with their probabilities as bars: 68%, 22%, 10%. These must sum to 100% over the full vocabulary (only the top three are shown).
  3. If the true next word is "mat", this position contributes -ln(0.68) = 0.386 nats. A confident correct prediction contributes little surprise; a confident wrong one contributes a lot. That asymmetry is the whole metric.

Common misunderstanding: lower perplexity does not mean a better model at everything. Perplexity measures next-token prediction on a specific corpus; downstream tasks (reasoning, instruction following) can diverge from it. It is the pretraining compass, not the final grade. Volume 11 covers what comes after.

"Perplexity measures surprise per token; calibration measures whether the confidence numbers mean what they say. You need both."

3.3 Lab 2.3: calibration in action

Lab 2.3: calibration (labs/lab_2_3_calibration.py)

Train a high-dimensional classifier to memorization (100% train accuracy), then measure what that does to its probabilities. Expected calibration error (ECE) bins predictions by confidence and averages the gap between confidence and accuracy. Temperature scaling (Guo et al., ICML 2017) divides all logits by a single fitted temperature T before the softmax: T > 1 softens overconfidence without changing any prediction, so accuracy is untouched.

Captured output (verbatim):

train accuracy:           100.00%   (memorized)
test accuracy:            83.29%   (unchanged by scaling)
ECE before calibration: 13.04%
fitted temperature T = 4.57  (T > 1 softens overconfidence)
ECE after calibration:  1.82%

confusion matrix: TP=1214 FP=253 FN=215 TN=1118
precision=0.828  recall=0.850  F1=0.838
How to read this diagram.
  1. Each panel is a reliability diagram: the x-axis is the model's stated confidence, the y-axis is its actual accuracy in that bin. The diagonal is perfect calibration.
  2. Before (left): bars sit below the diagonal at high confidence. The model says 95% and is right 80% of the time. ECE = 13.04%.
  3. After (right): with T = 4.57 the bars hug the diagonal. ECE = 1.82%. Accuracy did not move a tenth of a point: calibration is free once you measure it.

Reference: Chuan Guo, Geoff Pleiss, Yu Sun, Kilian Q. Weinberger, "On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks," ICML 2017 (arXiv:1706.04599). Their finding: modern networks, unlike older ones, are poorly calibrated, and temperature scaling, a single-parameter variant of Platt scaling, is surprisingly effective.

Key takeaways

  • Accuracy lies under class imbalance or unequal error costs; read the confusion matrix.
  • Perplexity is exponentiated cross-entropy: average surprise per token.
  • Modern networks are overconfident; measure ECE and fix it with temperature scaling.
  • Calibration never changes predictions, only the trustworthiness of the probabilities.

Chapter 4: Leakage: The Silent Killer

Design prompt

  • Define leakage in one sentence.
  • Name three ways leakage sneaks into a pipeline.
  • Your model hits 99% on a hard problem. What is your first move?
  • What is benchmark contamination, and why is it leakage at LLM scale?

4.1 The leakage taxonomy

Leakage is any path by which information about the test target reaches the model before evaluation. In one sentence: the model is graded on an exam it already saw. It is the silent killer because it inflates metrics without any visible error: the code runs, the loss falls, the test score is excellent, and the result is fiction.

Four species, each with a concrete shape. Target leakage: a feature that is a proxy for the label, like "days_since_purchase" predicting churn when it is computed from the future. Split contamination: near-duplicate rows landing on both sides of the split, so the test set contains training points in disguise. Temporal leakage: training on data from after the test period, letting the future inform predictions about it. Preprocessing leakage: fitting the scaler, the imputer, or the vocabulary on the full dataset before splitting, so test statistics shape the training inputs.

Under the hood, all four are the same bug: the independence assumption between train and test is violated, and the test score measures memorization of the leak rather than generalization. Concrete numbers from Lab 2.4: with all leaks in place the model scores 99.06%. After removing them, the honest score is 91.75%. The leak was worth 7.3 points of pure fiction.

How to read this diagram.
  1. The root is Leakage: test-target information reaching the model early.
  2. Target leak (coral): a feature that encodes the answer. The most direct and most embarrassing.
  3. Split contamination (amber): duplicates straddling the boundary. Your test set is your training set wearing a mask.
  4. Time leak (blue): future data training past predictions. Preprocess leak (teal): statistics fit on all the data before the split.

Common misunderstanding: "My test set is separate, so I am safe." Separation of rows is not enough. If the scaler was fit on all the data, if duplicates straddle the boundary, if a feature was computed with future knowledge, the rows are separate and the information is not.

"A 99% that surprises you is a leak until proven otherwise. Your first move is suspicion, not celebration."

4.2 Benchmark contamination: leakage at LLM scale

Benchmark contamination is leakage scaled up to pretraining: the evaluation benchmark, or near copies of it, ends up inside the model's training corpus. A model that has memorized the test questions does not demonstrate the capability the benchmark claims to measure. It demonstrates memorization, which is a different and much less useful skill.

How it happens: web-scale crawls swallow everything, including benchmark questions posted on GitHub, arXiv, forums, and dataset mirrors. How the field fights it: canary strings (unique markers embedded in benchmarks that crawlers are asked to exclude), training-data cutoff dates compared against benchmark release dates, and membership-inference style audits. None of these is airtight, which is why fresh, held-out, and private evaluations keep gaining importance.

Why this matters to you as a researcher: every public benchmark number you read is a number about a model whose training data you cannot fully audit. Treat public leaderboard scores as upper bounds on capability, and design your own evaluations with contamination in mind. Volume 11 builds the full methodology: private eval sets, temporal cutoffs, and decontamination checks as standard practice.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Left: the vast training data box. Right: the small benchmark box with its cracked shield.
  2. The coral arrow is the leak: benchmark content flowing into training through web crawls, mirrors, and reposts.
  3. The lesson: at LLM scale you cannot perfectly prevent this, so you defend in depth: canaries, cutoffs, audits, and private evals (Volume 11).

Common misunderstanding: "More training data is always better." Not if the extra data eats your evaluation. A benchmark inside the training set does not make the model smarter; it makes your measurement dumber.

"Every public benchmark score is an upper bound. Design your own evals assuming contamination, not hoping against it."

4.3 Lab 2.4: leakage detection in practice

Lab 2.4: leakage detection (labs/lab_2_4_leakage_detection.py)

A deliberately dirty pipeline: a target-leaking feature, duplicated rows straddling the split, and a scaler fit on all the data. Three detectors, then the honest re-run. The detectors are the point: build them into every pipeline you ever write.

Captured output (verbatim, detectors section):

naive test accuracy: 99.06%   <-- looks amazing

D1 single-feature scan (AUC of each feature alone):
   f0                     AUC = 0.838
   f1                     AUC = 0.772
   ...
   days_since_purchase    AUC = 1.000  <-- SUSPICIOUS

D2 duplicate audit:
   120 duplicated row-groups; 40 straddle the train/test boundary

D3 hygiene checklist:
   test indices inside train: 0 (must be 0)
   scaler fit on: ALL DATA (leak!) (must be 'train' only)

D1, the single-feature scan: train a trivial model on each feature alone. A real feature gets AUC 0.5-0.85; a feature with AUC = 1.000 is not a feature, it is the answer key. D2, the duplicate audit: hash rows and check whether identical groups land on both sides of the split. Here 40 of 120 duplicate groups straddle it. D3, the hygiene checklist: assert test indices are disjoint from train, and assert every preprocessing step was fit on train only. After fixing all three, the honest accuracy is 91.75%: the leak was worth 7.3 points.

Key takeaways

  • Leakage is test-target information reaching the model early; it inflates metrics silently.
  • Know the four species: target, split contamination, temporal, preprocessing.
  • Build the three detectors into every pipeline: single-feature scan, duplicate audit, hygiene checklist.
  • A surprising 99% is a leak until proven otherwise.

Chapter 5: Is the Win Real?

Design prompt

  • Your new model beats the old one by 1.2 points. Do you ship it?
  • What is a confidence interval actually telling you?
  • Why should comparisons be paired?
  • What is the difference between "not significant" and "no difference"?

5.1 Confidence intervals: quantifying the uncertainty

A confidence interval turns "B beats A by 1.2 points" into "the difference is plausibly anywhere from -0.3 to +2.7 points." The standard way to build one for a model comparison is the bootstrap: resample your test set with replacement a few thousand times, recompute the metric difference each time, and read off the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. No normality assumptions, no formulas to misremember, and it works for any metric.

Under the hood, the bootstrap treats your test set as a stand-in for the population and simulates the sampling wobble. What the 95% interval means, carefully: if you repeated the whole procedure many times, about 95% of the intervals would cover the true difference. It does not mean there is a 95% chance the truth is inside this particular interval. That misreading is the most common statistics error in ML, and reviewers love it.

Concrete numbers from Lab 2.5. Scenario 1: B beats A by +1.2 points, but the 95% CI is [-0.25, +2.70] and the p-value is 0.1236. The interval covers zero: not proven, ship nothing. Scenario 2: +4.5 points with CI [+3.10, +5.90], p = 0.0002. The interval excludes zero comfortably: a real win.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Each row is one comparison: the dot is the observed delta, the bar is the 95% bootstrap confidence interval.
  2. The vertical line at zero is the decision boundary. Scenario 1's bar crosses it: zero difference is plausible, so the win is not proven.
  3. Scenario 2's bar sits entirely right of zero: the win survives the uncertainty. That is the shape you need before you ship.

Common misunderstanding: "not significant" does not mean "no difference." It means the data cannot tell. Scenario 1 might be a real +1.2 win hiding in noise, or nothing at all. The honest statement is "not proven," not "disproven."

"Report the interval, not just the delta. If it crosses zero, you have a hypothesis, not a result."

5.2 Paired comparisons: removing the noise you can remove

Some noise you must live with; some you can subtract. When you compare models A and B, evaluate both on the same test examples and compare per-example outcomes. This is a paired comparison, and it removes the biggest source of variance for free: some examples are just harder than others, and that difficulty hits both models equally.

Under the hood: in an unpaired comparison, the variance of the difference includes the variance of example difficulty. In a paired comparison, each example serves as its own control, and the difficulty cancels out of the difference. The standard machinery is the paired permutation test: randomly flip the A/B labels within each pair a few thousand times, build the distribution of deltas under "no difference," and see where your observed delta lands. Lab 2.5 uses exactly this test.

The practical rule: never compare "A's accuracy on split 1" against "B's accuracy on split 2." Same data, same examples, both models, paired. It costs nothing and it is the difference between needing 10,000 test examples and needing 2,000.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Unpaired (left): model A's scores and model B's scores are two separate clouds. Example difficulty inflates both clouds' spread.
  2. Paired (right): each line connects one example's A-score to its B-score. The comparison is now about the lines' directions, and shared difficulty cancels.
  3. Same data, tighter conclusion. Pairing is free statistical power: always pair when you can.

Common misunderstanding: running a t-test on two accuracy numbers (one per model) is meaningless: n = 2 has no variance estimate. The units of a paired test are the examples (or the seeds), not the models.

"Same examples, both models, paired test. Example difficulty is noise you can subtract, so subtract it."

Q3. A paper reports "Model B beats Model A, 81.2% vs 80.1%, p < 0.05 by t-test on 5 seeds each." What is the strongest objection, and what would you ask for instead?

Answer: the t-test is on 5+5 seed-means, which conflates seed noise with the model difference and may use different data splits per seed. Ask for a paired comparison: both models evaluated on the same examples (or same seeded splits), with a paired permutation test or bootstrap CI on the per-example differences.

  • "The p-value is wrong," wrong: the p-value may be computed correctly; the problem is the experimental design feeding it.
  • "Unpaired design wastes power and mixes variance sources," right: pairing on the same examples removes difficulty variance.

5.3 Lab 2.5: the win-real test

Lab 2.5: significance (labs/lab_2_5_significance.py)

Two scenarios, same machinery: bootstrap 95% CI on the accuracy difference plus a paired permutation p-value. Scenario 1 is a small noisy win; scenario 2 is a larger cleaner win. The lab's job is to make you feel the difference between "positive delta" and "proven win."

Captured output (verbatim):

--- Scenario 1: B net +24 examples (+1.2 pp), noisy disagreements ---
A: 79.40%   B: 80.60%   raw delta: +1.20 pp
bootstrap 95% CI on the difference: [-0.25, +2.70] pp
paired permutation p-value: 0.1236
verdict: NOT PROVEN: the interval covers 0. Ship nothing on this.

--- Scenario 2: B net +90 examples (+4.5 pp), cleaner signal ---
A: 80.85%   B: 85.35%   raw delta: +4.50 pp
bootstrap 95% CI on the difference: [+3.10, +5.90] pp
paired permutation p-value: 0.0002
verdict: REAL WIN: interval excludes 0 and p < 0.05

Notice what the lab does not say about scenario 1: it does not say B is worse or equal. It says the data cannot tell. That humility is the skill.

Key takeaways

  • Report the interval on the difference, not just the delta.
  • If the 95% CI covers zero, the win is not proven: ship nothing on it.
  • "Not significant" means "cannot tell," not "no difference."
  • Always pair: same examples, both models, paired test. It is free power.

Where this leads: Volume 4 takes the normalization and mixed-precision ideas from Volume 3 to transformer scale, and Volume 11 builds full evaluation methodology for LLM systems on the statistics you learned here: paired comparisons, private eval sets, and contamination-aware benchmarking.
